(Those who feed meat every evening, until the sun sets into the heaving sea.)
(مَلْعُونِينَ): In al-Asās and al-Lisān he said: «لعنه أهله: his people drove him out and put him far away; he is laʿīn, an outcast. Allah cursed Iblīs: He drove him out of Paradise and put him far from the neighbourhood of the angels. لعنت الكلب والذئب: I drove them both away; the wolf is called al-laʿīn. لعّنه, and he is mulaʿʿan: he cursed him much. تلاعن القوم, تلعّنوا and التعنوا; التعن فلان: he cursed himself. A man who is luʿna and laʿana, like ḍuḥka and ḍuḥaka [one who is cursed by people / one who curses much]. Do not be laʿʿān, i.e. a reviler. لاعن امرأته [he performed the mutual cursing with his wife], and the judge conducted the mutual cursing between them; al-liʿān took place between them, and they cursed one another (تلاعنا والتعنا). Among the figurative usages: أبيت اللعن, which was the greeting of kings in the Jāhiliyya, i.e. may you not do anything that would bring on cursing; and so-and-so is mulaʿʿan al-qidr (his cooking-pot is cursed). Zuhayr said:
ومرهّق النيران يحمد في اللأ ... واء غير ملعّن القدر
(One whose fires are sought by guests, praised in hardship, his cooking-pot not cursed.)
He set up al-laʿīn in his field, which is the scarecrow; and the accursed tree: everyone who tasted it cursed it and hated it».
(ثُقِفُوا): they were found and overtaken. In al-Asās: «We sought him and ثقفناه in such a place, i.e. we caught him. ثقفت العلم أو الصناعة in the quickest time: when you are quick in acquiring it. A boy who is thaqf laqf and thaqif laqif [quick to grasp and to catch]; he has become skilful (thaqufa thaqāfa). ثاقفه مثاقفة: he sported with him with weapons, which is trying to catch the other off guard in sword-play and the like; so-and-so is of the people of muthāqafa, and he is a muthāqif: good at thiqāf with the sword, with kasra. They fenced with one another and so-and-so was the most skilful of them. خلّ ثقيف and ثقّيف: sharp vinegar; in Kitāb al-ʿAyn: ثقيف, and it has become sharp (thaqufa thaqāfa). Among the figurative usages: he educated him and refined him (ثقّفه); were it not for your refining and guiding me I would have been nothing; was I cultivated and refined except at your hand?». The wording of al-Qāmūs: «ثقف, like karuma and fariḥa, thaqfan, thaqafan and thaqāfatan: he became skilful, nimble and astute; so he is thaqf, like ḥibr, thaqif, like katif, and thaqīf, like amīr».

* I'rab:
(لَئِنْ لَمْ يَنْتَهِ الْمُنافِقُونَ وَالَّذِينَ فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ): the lām prepares for the oath (al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾa lil-qasam); إن is conditional; لم is a particle of negation, conversion [to the past] and jussive; ينته is an imperfect verb, jussive (majzūm) by لم, and it stands as the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ). المنافقون is its fāʿil (agent); الذين is conjoined to المنافقون; في قلوبهم is a fronted khabar (predicate) and مرض a postponed mubtadaʾ (subject), and the nominal clause is the ṣila (relative clause) of the relative noun.
(وَالْمُرْجِفُونَ فِي الْمَدِينَةِ لَنُغْرِيَنَّكَ بِهِمْ): والمرجفون is also conjoined, thereby completing the three descriptions of one thing; for they were three kinds: among them the hypocrites, the people of depravity sick of heart, and those who spread evil reports about the expeditions of the Messenger of Allah — or it is general, covering every rumour-mongering and fabrication of evil reports. في المدينة is attached (mutaʿalliq) to المرجفون. The lām occurs in the answer to the oath, and the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is omitted, indicated by the answer to the oath. نغرينك is an imperfect verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa because it is joined to the heavy nūn of emphasis; the fāʿil is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "نحن"; the kāf is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), and بهم is attached to نغرينك.
(ثُمَّ لا يُجاوِرُونَكَ فِيها إِلَّا قَلِيلًا): ثم is a conjunction of sequence with delay. The conjunction indicating delay was preferred only because expulsion from their homelands was graver for them than everything else that befell them, so its status is distanced from the status of what it is conjoined to. In it there is an indication that one who is lawfully required to vacate a dwelling owned by another is given respite while he moves himself, his goods and his family, for a period of time until he obtains another dwelling, according to [the judge's] discretion. لا is negative; يجاورونك is an imperfect verb conjoined to نغرينك, so it is nominative, the sign of its nominative being the retention of the nūn; the wāw is its fāʿil and the kāf its object. فيها is attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial). إلا is a particle of restriction, and قليلا is an adverb of time attached to يجاورونك, or a maṣdar — i.e. except a [little] neighbouring — i.e. a short time while they depart and gather themselves and their families.
(مَلْعُونِينَ أَيْنَما ثُقِفُوا أُخِذُوا وَقُتِّلُوا تَقْتِيلًا): ملعونين is a ḥāl of something implied which has been omitted together with its governing word, i.e. then they will go out [accursed]; or of the fāʿil of يجاورونك, the particle of exception having entered upon the adverb and the ḥāl together, as in His words «إلا أن يؤذن لكم إلى طعام غير ناظرين إناه». Al-Zamakhsharī said:
«It is not valid for it to be made accusative by أخذوا, because what comes after the conditional word does not govern what comes before it. It has been said of قليلا that it too is accusative as a ḥāl, its meaning being: they will not be your neighbours except as few, humiliated and accursed». Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ allowed it to be made accusative by أخذوا, because they both allow the governed word of the apodosis to be put before the conditional particle, as in: خيرا إن تأتيني تصب. أينما is a jussive conditional noun in the position of the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarfiyya makāniyya), and it is attached to أخذوا, i.e. to its apodosis. ثقفوا is a passive past verb, in the position of the jussive as the protasis; أخذوا is also a passive past verb, and it is the apodosis; قتلوا is a passive past verb, and تقتيلا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object).
(سُنَّةَ اللَّهِ فِي الَّذِينَ خَلَوْا مِنْ قَبْلُ وَلَنْ تَجِدَ لِسُنَّةِ اللَّهِ تَبْدِيلًا): سنة الله is in the position of the accusative as a maṣdar, i.e. it is an emphatic maṣdar, i.e. Allah has laid down concerning those who act hypocritically that they be killed wherever they are caught. في الذين is a ḥāl; the clause خلوا is the ṣila; من قبل is attached to خلوا. ولن: the wāw is a conjunction, though you may make it circumstantial; لن is a particle of negation, accusative and futurity; تجد is an imperfect verb, accusative by لن; لسنة الله is attached to تبديلا; تبديلا is a mafʿūl bihi.
(يَسْئَلُكَ النَّاسُ عَنِ السَّاعَةِ): a resumptive statement, introduced to relate the state of the mockers among the polytheists and the Jews, who used to ask the Prophet about the Hour, seeking to hasten it by way of mockery. يسألك is an imperfect verb and a fronted mafʿūl bihi; الناس is the fāʿil; عن الساعة is attached to يسألك.
(قُلْ إِنَّما عِلْمُها عِنْدَ اللَّهِ): إنما is the restraining [ما] and the restrained [إن] (kāffa wa-makfūfa); علمها is a mubtadaʾ, and عند الله is an adverb of place attached to an omitted khabar.
(وَما يُدْرِيكَ لَعَلَّ السَّاعَةَ تَكُونُ قَرِيباً): the wāw is a conjunction; ما is an interrogative noun of disapproval, a mubtadaʾ, and the clause يدريك is its khabar. لعل and its noun, and the clause تكون is its khabar; the clause is suspended (muʿallaqa) by the interrogative, so it is in the position of the accusative as a second object. قريبا is the khabar of تكون, on the basis that the qualified noun is omitted, i.e. something near. وقل قريبا [Translator's note: so in the source; presumably وقيل, "It has been said"]: its use as an adverb has become frequent, so here it is an adverb in the position of the khabar. Al-Zamakhsharī indicated the two views by saying: «قريبا: something near; or because the Hour has the sense of the Day; or [it means] at a near time».

dervis-irab:64-68.t:
* Vocabulary:
(سادَتَنا): a broken plural on the pattern faʿala, with two fatḥas. This pattern is common for an adjective describing a rational masculine being whose final radical is sound, as كامل / كملة, ساحر / سحرة, سافر / سفرة and بار / بررة. Allah the Exalted said: «وجاء السحرة» and «بأيدي سفرة، كرام بررة». The condition "adjective" excludes the noun, as واد and باز; "masculine" excludes words like حائض and طالق; "rational" excludes words like سابق and لاحق as descriptions of two horses; and "sound final radical" excludes words like قاض and غاز. None of these is regularly pluralised on faʿala with two fatḥas. It occurs anomalously with words not of the pattern fāʿil, as سيد / سادة, whose pattern is faʿala. It may also be the plural of سائد, like فاجر / فجرة and كافر / كفرة, and this is closer to analogy, as you have seen. Yet the author of al-Qāmūs did not keep to the rule, for he said: «al-sāʾid is the master, or one below him, and the plural is سادة and سيايد». Ibn ʿĀmir read ساداتنا, pluralising it a second time with alif and tāʾ, and this too is not according to analogy.

* I'rab:
(إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَعَنَ الْكافِرِينَ وَأَعَدَّ لَهُمْ سَعِيراً): إن and its noun, and the clause لعن الكافرين is its khabar (predicate). أعد is conjoined to لعن; لهم is attached (mutaʿalliq) to أعدّ; سعيرا is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object). Al-saʿīr is the fire that is kindled, intensely blazing, and for that reason the pronoun referring to it is feminine.
(خالِدِينَ فِيها أَبَداً لا يَجِدُونَ وَلِيًّا وَلا نَصِيراً): a ḥāl (circumstantial) of الكافرين. فيها is attached to خالدين, and أبدا is an adverb of time also attached to خالدين. The clause لا يجدون is a second ḥāl; وليا is the object of يجدون, and ولا نصيرا is conjoined to وليا.
(يَوْمَ تُقَلَّبُ وُجُوهُهُمْ فِي النَّارِ يَقُولُونَ يا لَيْتَنا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَا): يوم is an adverb of time attached to يقولون, or attached to an omitted verb whose implied form is "اذكر" (remember). Abū al-Baqāʾ attached it to His words لا يجدون or to نصيرا. The clause تقلب is in the position of the genitive by the adverb's annexation to it; it is a passive imperfect verb, and وجوههم is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent); في النار is attached to تقلب. The clause يقولون is either resumptive or a ḥāl of the pronoun in وجوههم or of the faces themselves. The secret of singling out the faces and the meaning of their being turned will come in the Rhetoric section. يا is a particle of alerting, or a vocative particle with the one addressed omitted. ليت and its noun, and the clause أطعنا الله is its khabar; وأطعنا الرسولا is conjoined to أطعنا الله.
(وَقالُوا رَبَّنا إِنَّا أَطَعْنا سادَتَنا وَكُبَراءَنا فَأَضَلُّونَا السَّبِيلَا): a resumptive statement, introduced to lay out an excuse for themselves. You may also conjoin it to يقولون, by way of turning from the imperfect to the past to indicate that this saying of theirs is not continuous like their previous saying, but is a kind of excuse that is neither valid nor accepted. ربنا is a vocative in construct (munādā muḍāf); إن and its noun, and the clause أطعنا سادتنا وكبراءنا is its khabar. فأضلونا is conjoined to أطعنا; أضلونا is a past verb, its fāʿil (agent) and first mafʿūl bihi, and السبيلا is the second mafʿūl bihi; one says ضل السبيل and أضله إياه. The alif is added to prolong the sound; the verse-endings were made like the rhymes of poetry, and its benefit is the pause and the indication that the speech has ended and that what follows is resumptive.
(رَبَّنا آتِهِمْ ضِعْفَيْنِ مِنَ الْعَذابِ وَالْعَنْهُمْ لَعْناً كَبِيراً): آتهم is an imperative verb, a latent (mustatir) fāʿil and a first mafʿūl bihi; ضعفين is the second mafʿūl bihi; من العذاب is an adjective of ضعفين. العنهم is an imperative verb, a latent fāʿil and a mafʿūl bihi; لعنا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object), and كبيرا is a naʿt (adjective) of لعنا.

* Rhetoric:
In His words «يوم تقلب وجوههم في النار», the faces are singled out for mention because the face is above all the other limbs, and it stands as that which confronts [others]. The meaning of their being turned is their being turned about in different directions, like meat roasted in the fire, or [like something] placed in the water of a pot while it is boiling, so that the boiling tosses it to every side.

dervis-irab:18-19.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْمُعَوِّقِينَ): those who discourage, who used to let the Muslims down. In al-Asās: «عاقه, اعتاقه and عوّقه (he hindered him): "قد يعلم الله المعوّقين منكم". And you say: "So-and-so kept company with hindrance (التعويق), so success (التوفيق) abandoned him." A man who is عُوَقة is one given to hindering and holding back from good. And you say: "O you who holds back from good, the most fitting of your names is 'ʿAwwaq'."» [Translator's note: the last phrase is a pun in the Arabic, «أن تعوق», which may be read as the idol's name Yaʿūq/ʿAwūq or as "that you hinder".]
(أَشِحَّةً): plural of (شحيح), the miserly and covetous. It is a non-analogical plural, because the analogical plural of the adjective of the pattern فعيل whose second and third radicals are of the same kind (i.e. doubled) is أفعلاء, as in خليل / أخلاء and ظنين / أظناء; and أشحاء has been heard, which is the analogical form.
(سَلَقُوكُمْ): they hurt you, or harmed you. In al-Mukhtār: «سلقه بالكلام: he hurt him with words, which is harshness of speech with the tongue; the Exalted said: "سلقوكم بألسنة حداد". سلق البقل أو البيض: he boiled the herbs or the eggs lightly over the fire. All of them are of the conjugation of ضرب.» In al-Miṣbāḥ it is also of the conjugation of قتل. Al-Rāghib's wording: «السلق is stretching out with force, either with the hand or with the tongue.» And it is taken from al-Qāmūs and al-Lisān: سلق, يسلق, of the conjugation of قتل: he boiled the eggs or the herbs over the fire and cooked them in water; سلقه بالكلام: he hurt him — and from this, سلقه بألسنة حداد; سلقه بالرمح: he pierced him with the spear; سلقه بالسوط: he whipped him until he stripped off his skin; سلق اللحم عن العظم: he peeled the meat off the bone. The expression may be figurative, as will come in the section on rhetoric. In any case, the common people use this word in a way that is beyond reproach.

* I'rab:
(قَدْ يَعْلَمُ اللَّهُ الْمُعَوِّقِينَ مِنْكُمْ وَالْقائِلِينَ لِإِخْوانِهِمْ هَلُمَّ إِلَيْنا): resumptive speech, introduced to depict the state of the hypocrites. (قد) is a particle of multiplicity, though its basic sense is paucity when it enters an imperfect verb; its discussion has preceded. (يعلم الله المعوقين) is a verb, its fāʿil (agent) and its mafʿūl bihi (direct object); (منكم) is a ḥāl (circumstantial); (القائلين) is conjoined to (المعوقين); (لإخوانهم) is attached to (mutaʿalliq) (القائلين). (هلم) is a verbal noun with imperative meaning, and (إلينا) is attached to it. This is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, who make it the same for the singular and the plural; it is used intransitively, as here, and transitively, as in al-Anʿām, and the discussion of it has preceded. (وَلا يَأْتُونَ الْبَأْسَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا): the wāw is circumstantial; (لا) is negating; (يأتون البأس) is an imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ), its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi — i.e. the fighting; (إلا) is a particle of restriction, and (قليلا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) or an adverb of time. (أَشِحَّةً عَلَيْكُمْ فَإِذا جاءَ الْخَوْفُ رَأَيْتَهُمْ يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَيْكَ): (أشحة) is a ḥāl from the fāʿil of (يأتون), or accusative in censure by an omitted verb, its implied form being "I censure" (أذم). Al-Zamakhsharī's wording: «أشحة عليكم: at the time of war, sparing of you [Translator's note: the source has «أضناء», apparently for «أضنّاء»], hovering over you as a man does over the one who defends him and fights on his behalf at a time of fear.» (فإذا): the fāʾ is resumptive, and (إذا) is a future adverb including the sense of condition; the clause (جاء الخوف) is in the position of a genitive, the adverb being put in construct with it. The clause (رأيتهم) has no grammatical position, because it is the apodosis of a non-jussive condition. The clause (ينظرون إليك) is a ḥāl, because the seeing here is visual; (إليك) is attached to (ينظرون).
(تَدُورُ أَعْيُنُهُمْ كَالَّذِي يُغْشى عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْمَوْتِ): the clause (تدور أعينهم) is a ḥāl from the fāʿil of (ينظرون), which is the wāw. (كالذي) is the naʿt (adjective) of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. "they roll a rolling like the rolling of the eye of the one who…"; so after the kāf two things are omitted: "rolling" and "eye". The clause (يغشى) is the ṣila (relative clause) of (الذي). (يغشى) is an imperfect verb in the passive, and the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) is the pronoun of a maṣdar, made specific by the lām of prior reference or by an omitted adjective, the meaning being "the familiar swooning comes over him"; (عليه) is attached to (يغشى). The nāʾib fāʿil may also be the preposition with its genitive noun; the discussion of what stands in for the nāʾib fāʿil has preceded, so refresh your memory of it. (فَإِذا ذَهَبَ الْخَوْفُ سَلَقُوكُمْ بِأَلْسِنَةٍ حِدادٍ): the fāʾ is a conjunction; (إذا) is a future adverb including the sense of condition; the clause (ذهب الخوف) is in the position of a genitive, the adverb being put in construct with it. The clause (سلقوكم) is the apodosis of a non-jussive condition, with no grammatical position; (بألسنة) is attached to (سلقوكم), and (حداد) is the naʿt of (ألسنة).
(أَشِحَّةً عَلَى الْخَيْرِ أُولئِكَ لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا فَأَحْبَطَ اللَّهُ أَعْمالَهُمْ وَكانَ ذلِكَ عَلَى اللَّهِ يَسِيراً): (أشحة) is accusative as a ḥāl or in censure, as preceded. (على الخير) is attached to (أشحة), i.e. greedy for the booty, seeking it. (أولئك) is the mubtadaʾ (subject) and the clause (لم يؤمنوا) is the khabar (predicate). (فأحبط) is conjoined to (لم يؤمنوا); (الله) is the fāʿil and (أعمالهم) the mafʿūl bihi. (وكان): the wāw is circumstantial or resumptive; (كان) with its noun and its khabar; (على الله) is a ḥāl. The demonstrative refers to the nullifying, and the meaning is that their deeds deserve to be nullified, with nothing to avert it, and it is not a hard or difficult matter.

* Rhetoric:
1- The device of al-tandīr (the witty touch):
In His saying «فإذا جاء الخوف رأيتهم ينظرون إليك تدور أعينهم كالذي يغشى عليه الموت» [Translator's note: so in the source; the verse reads «يُغْشى عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْمَوْتِ»] there is a device alluded to by the author of Nihāyat al-Arab and by Ibn Abī al-Iṣbaʿ, namely the device of al-tandīr. Its definition is that the speaker brings a sweet rarity or a delightful witticism. It occurs in both earnest and jest; it does not fall within the scope of sarcasm, nor within the scope of the jest that intends earnest, but it may fall within the scope of hyperbole. That is clear in the Exalted's hyperbole in describing the hypocrites with fear and cowardice, where He reported of them that their eyes roll while looking, like the state of one who swoons from death. Had He confined Himself to saying "like one who swoons" it would have sufficed for the purpose, but He added something by saying «من الموت», since the state of one swooning from death is more severe and more grievous than the state of one swooning from something other than death. Had He, glory be to Him, put "fear" in place of "death", the speech would certainly have been eloquent; yet what came in the Revelation is more eloquent. It is, moreover, framed as truth and set in the place of veracity, for whoever is strong of soul and brave of heart does not accept hypocrisy, but openly shows what the fearful one conceals, because he does not care about death.
2- The implicit metaphor (al-istiʿāra al-makniyya):
That is in His saying «سلقوكم بألسنة حداد»: He likened the tongue to a sword, then omitted the thing compared to and borrowed one of its properties, namely striking. This metaphor holds on the interpretation of السلق as striking, and what prompts it is the description of the tongues as sharp, as preceded in the section on vocabulary.

dervis-irab:20-22.t:
* Vocabulary:
(بادُونَ): plural of (باد), a dweller of the desert. One says: "You have gone to the desert (بدوت), so-and-so", i.e. you have settled in the desert and become a Bedouin; "What have you to do with Bedouin life?"; and "the town-dweller became a Bedouin (تبدّى)". One says: "Where are the people?" and you say: "They have gone out to the desert (لقد بدوا)", i.e. they went out to the open country — they had a few sheep they would go out to.
(الْأَعْرابِ): He said in al-Qāmūs and its commentary: al-ʿurb, with ḍamma, and al-ʿarab, with fatḥa on both letters, are the opposite of the non-Arabs (al-ʿajam); it is feminine. They are the inhabitants of the towns, or it is general; and al-aʿrāb among them are the inhabitants of the desert; it has no singular, and its plural is أعاريب. "ʿArab ʿāriba", "ʿarbāʾ" and "ʿaraba" are pure Arabs; "mutaʿarriba" and "mustaʿriba" are those who entered among them.

* I'rab:
(يَحْسَبُونَ الْأَحْزابَ لَمْ يَذْهَبُوا وَإِنْ يَأْتِ الْأَحْزابُ يَوَدُّوا لَوْ أَنَّهُمْ بادُونَ فِي الْأَعْرابِ): the speech is resumptive, introduced to depict their fear. You may make it a ḥāl (circumstantial) from one of the preceding pronouns, i.e. from fear they are like those who cannot believe that the Confederates have gone away from them and abandoned supporting them.
(يحسبون) is an imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ), and the wāw is the fāʿil (agent); (الأحزاب) is the first mafʿūl bihi (direct object), and the clause (لم يذهبوا) is the second mafʿūl bihi. (وإن): the wāw is a conjunction and (إن) is conditional; (يأت) is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ), jussive (majzūm), the sign of its jussive being the dropping of the weak letter; (الأحزاب) is the fāʿil; (يودوا) is the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ), jussive, the sign of its jussive being the dropping of the nūn. (لو) is maṣdariyya (forming a maṣdar); (لو) and what follows it are interpreted as a maṣdar that is the object of (يودوا), i.e. because of their fear of what they have been afflicted with they wish their being [Translator's note: the source has «أشرتهم», which appears corrupt; perhaps «كونهم»] out in the desert. And (أن) with what falls in its domain is interpreted as a maṣdar that is the fāʿil of an omitted verb, its implied form being "they would wish that it were established that they are in the desert". More discussion of maṣdariyya (لو) will come in the section on benefits. (أن) with its noun, and (بادون) is its khabar (predicate); (في الأعراب) is attached to (mutaʿalliq) (بادون), or to an omitted ḥāl.
(يَسْئَلُونَ عَنْ أَنْبائِكُمْ وَلَوْ كانُوا فِيكُمْ ما قاتَلُوا إِلَّا قَلِيلًا): the clause (يسألون) may be resumptive, or a ḥāl from the pronoun of (يحسبون). (عن أنبائكم) is attached to (يسألون). The wāw is circumstantial; (لو) is conditional; (كان) with its noun, and (فيكم) is its khabar. (ما) is negating; (قاتلوا) is a verb and its fāʿil; the clause (ما قاتلوا) has no grammatical position, because it is the apodosis of a non-jussive condition. What we set out regarding His saying «ولو أن ما في البحر من شجرة أقلام» — the verse — applies to it. (إلا) is a particle of restriction, and (قليلا) is the naʿt (adjective) of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. "except a little fighting", or the naʿt of an omitted adverb, i.e. "except a little time".
(لَقَدْ كانَ لَكُمْ فِي رَسُولِ اللَّهِ أُسْوَةٌ حَسَنَةٌ): resumptive speech, introduced to reproach those who stayed behind from fighting. The lām is the answer to an omitted oath, and (قد) is a particle of verification. (كان) is a defective past verb; (لكم) is its fronted khabar; (في رسول الله) is a ḥāl, because it was originally an adjective of (أسوة); (أسوة) is the delayed noun of (كان), and (حسنة) is an adjective of (أسوة), i.e. a good example — with ḍamma on the hamza, and it may take kasra.
(لِمَنْ كانَ يَرْجُوا اللَّهَ وَالْيَوْمَ الْآخِرَ وَذَكَرَ اللَّهَ كَثِيراً): (لمن): the preposition with its genitive noun is a badal (substitute) from (لكم), the lām being repeated with the badal for separation; or it is a badal al-ishtimāl (substitute of inclusion). The clause (كان) is the ṣila (relative clause) of (من); the noun of (كان) is latent, its implied form being "he", and the clause (يرجو الله) is its khabar. (اليوم الآخر) is conjoined to the Divine Name; (ذكر) is conjoined to (كان); the Divine Name is the mafʿūl bihi, and (كثيرا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) or an adverb; its like has preceded shortly.
(وَلَمَّا رَأَ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الْأَحْزابَ قالُوا: هذا ما وَعَدَنَا اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ): (لما) is a temporal adverb (ḥīniyya) attached to (قالوا), or a linking particle including the sense of condition, in either case. (رأى المؤمنون الأحزاب) is a past verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; the clause (قالوا) has no grammatical position. (هذا) is the mubtadaʾ (subject) and (ما) the khabar, and the clause is the maqūl al-qawl (object of the saying); the clause (وعدنا الله ورسوله) is the ṣila of (ما). (وَصَدَقَ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ وَما زادَهُمْ إِلَّا إِيماناً وَتَسْلِيماً): the wāw is a conjunction; (صدق الله) is a verb and its fāʿil. In it the overt noun is put in place of the pronoun, to magnify Him and to draw attention to the promise of the two of them that came to pass. (وما زادهم) is conjoined to (صدق); (إلا) is a particle of restriction; (إيمانا) is the second mafʿūl bihi of (زادهم), and (تسليما) is conjoined to (إيمانا). The fāʿil of (زادهم) is the pronoun of the promise, or of the truthfulness.

* Rhetoric:
In His saying «وصدق الله ورسوله» there is the device of repeating the overt noun out of veneration. Had He repeated the two as pronouns, He would have combined the name of Allah the Exalted and the name of His Messenger in one word, saying «وصدقا» ("and the two were truthful"). The Prophet disliked that, when he answered one of the preachers who spoke before him, who said: "Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger is rightly guided, and whoever disobeys the two of them (يعصهما) has gone astray." The Prophet said to him: "What a bad preacher of the people you are! Say: 'and whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger'", aiming to magnify Allah. Some scholars found a difficulty in his saying, upon him be blessing and peace, "until Allah and His Messenger are more beloved to him than anything besides the two of them (سواهما)", saying that he combined them in a single pronoun. This difficulty was answered by saying that the Prophet ﷺ knows Allah's due better than we do, so it is not for us to say as he says.

* Benefits:
Maṣdariyya (لو):
Maṣdariyya (لو) is synonymous with maṣdariyya (أن) in meaning and in forming a maṣdar, except that it does not put the verb in the accusative. It occurs mostly after something with the sense of wishing, such as ودّ, أحب, اختار and تمنى; and it is said, rather, specifically after ودّ and تمنى, because a person may love a thing yet not wish for its occurrence owing to some obstacle in seeking it. It occurs after other than wishing rarely, as in the saying of Qutayla — in the diminutive form — daughter of al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith al-Asadiyya, addressing the Prophet ﷺ when he had her father al-Naḍr killed in captivity (ṣabran) after returning from the Battle of Badr:
ما كان ضرك المن لو مننت وربما ... منّ الفتى وهو المغيظ المحنق
(What harm would it have done you had you shown grace? Often a young man shows grace though enraged and furious.)
i.e. "what would grace have harmed you" [Translator's note: the source glosses the verse as «ما كان ضرك المن», showing the maṣdar meaning of «لو مننت»]. Before this verse is:
أمحمد ولأنت فحل نجيبة ... في قومها والفحل فحل معرق
(O Muhammad — you are the scion of a noble mother among her people, and the stallion is of a deep-rooted stallion line.)
The reason the Prophet had her father killed was that he used to read the stories of the Persians to the Arabs, saying: "Muhammad brings you the stories of ʿĀd and Thamūd, and I bring you the story of the Chosroes and the Caesars", intending thereby to hurt the Prophet. When the Prophet heard this verse — one of a set of verses she recited before him — he said: "Had I heard it before his killing, I would not have killed him, and I would have pardoned him." Then he said: "No Qurashī shall be killed in captivity."
Some legal theorists have taken his saying ﷺ "Had I heard it before his killing, I would not have killed him, and I would have pardoned him" as evidence for the permissibility of delegating judgment to the mujtahid — so that it is said to him: "Judge as you will, and it is right" — and for its having actually occurred; for his saying "before his killing" indicates that the killing and its omission were delegated to him. Those who deny its occurrence answer that it is possible the Prophet was given a choice between the two together, so it was said to him: "You may order his killing or not order it", and the like; and it is possible that revelation came down that, had someone interceded for him, he would not have killed him. The نجيبة is the noble, good woman; the فحل is the male of every animal, as in al-Qāmūs; and معرق is the active participle of أعرق الرجل, "the man became deep-rooted", i.e. he has a root in nobility. The meaning of (لو مننت) is "had you bestowed a favour and done good". Then it is possible that the interpreted maṣdar from (لو) and (مننت), i.e. "the grace", is the delayed noun of (كان), and the clause (ضرك) its fronted khabar; and it is possible that the maṣdar is the fāʿil of (ضرك), the clause being the khabar of (كان), whose noun is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn). It is also possible that (ما) is interrogative, its position nominative as a mubtadaʾ, and (كان) may be redundant (zāʾida) or not: on the first, the clause (ضرك) is the khabar of interrogative (ما); on the second, the clause (ضرك) is the khabar of (كان) and the clause of (كان) is the khabar of (ما). Moreover, it is possible that (لو) is conditional in its normal use, with what precedes indicating the apodosis — and that would overturn all of this. (المغيظ), with fatḥa on the mīm, is the passive participle of غاظه يغيظه, with the dotted ghayn and ẓāʾ — the غيظ being anger, or its intensity, or its first onset. (المحنق), with ḍamma on the mīm and fatḥa on the nūn, is the passive participle of أحنقه, with the undotted ḥāʾ, when he enraged him.
Returning to the mention of maṣdariyya (لو), we say: maṣdariyya (لو) has no apodosis; when a past verb follows it, it remains past, and when an imperfect verb follows it, it makes it purely future — just as maṣdariyya (أن) does.

dervis-irab:23-27.t:
* Vocabulary:
(قَضى نَحْبَهُ): he died. النحب is a vow (النذر), and their saying "he fulfilled his naḥb" has come to be an expression for death, because every living being must die, so it is as though it were a binding vow upon his neck; when he dies, he has fulfilled his naḥb, i.e. his vow. النذر is with fatḥa on the nūn; the author of al-Munjid erred in vocalising it with kasra, and that is strange. In al-Miṣbāḥ: «نحب نحبا, of the conjugation of ضرب: he wept, and the noun is النحيب; نحب نحبا, of the conjugation of قتل: he vowed. قضى نحبه: he died, or was killed in the way of Allah. In the Revelation: "فمنهم من قضى نحبه".»
(صَياصِيهِمْ): their fortresses; plural of صيصية. In al-Qāmūs: «The صيصية is the weaver's spike with which the warp and weft are evened, the spur on the rooster's leg, the horn of cattle and gazelles, the fortress, and anything by which one is protected.»

* I'rab:
(مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ رِجالٌ صَدَقُوا ما عاهَدُوا اللَّهَ عَلَيْهِ): resumptive speech, introduced to set out the state of the righteous among the Companions who vowed that, if they met a battle alongside the Messenger of Allah, they would stand firm and fight until they were martyred, and to divide them into two groups.
(من المؤمنين) is a fronted khabar (predicate) and (رجال) a delayed mubtadaʾ (subject); the clause (صدقوا) is an adjective of (رجال); (ما) is a relative noun, the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); (عاهدوا الله عليه) is the ṣila (relative clause) of (ما), and (عليه) is attached to (mutaʿalliq) (عاهدوا). (فَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ قَضى نَحْبَهُ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَنْتَظِرُ وَما بَدَّلُوا تَبْدِيلًا): the fāʾ is of ramification (tafrīʿ); (منهم) is a fronted khabar and (من) a delayed mubtadaʾ; the clause (قضى نحبه) is the ṣila of (من); (ومنهم من ينتظر) is conjoined to what precedes it. The wāw is a conjunction, (ما) is negating, (بدلوا) is a verb and its fāʿil (agent), and the mafʿūl bihi is omitted, i.e. the pledge; (تبديلا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object). (لِيَجْزِيَ اللَّهُ الصَّادِقِينَ بِصِدْقِهِمْ وَيُعَذِّبَ الْمُنافِقِينَ إِنْ شاءَ): the lām is the lām of cause; (يجزي) is an imperfect verb, accusative (manṣūb) by an implied (أن) after the lām. The preposition with its genitive noun is attached to an implied resumptive verb, introduced to explain what brought about the occurrence of the sayings that were narrated, the implied form being "all that occurred, occurred so that Allah may reward the truthful". It is also said to be attached to what precedes it and to follow from it, so that it is attached to (صدقوا), as a cause for it; and other things have been said, but what we have mentioned is preferable. (الله) is the fāʿil, (الصادقين) the mafʿūl bihi, and (بصدقهم) is attached to (يجزي). (ويعذب المنافقين) is conjoined to (ليجزي الله الصادقين). (إن) is conditional; (شاء) is a past verb, the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ), and the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is omitted, as is the object of (شاء), i.e. "if He wills to punish them, He punishes them".
(أَوْ يَتُوبَ عَلَيْهِمْ إِنَّ اللَّهَ كانَ غَفُوراً رَحِيماً): (أو) is a conjunction and (يتوب) is conjoined to what precedes it; (عليهم) is attached to (يتوب). The clause (إن الله) is a causal explanation of what precedes: (إن) with its noun, and the clause (كان) is its khabar; the noun of (كان) is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "He"; (غفورا) is its first khabar and (رحيما) its second khabar.
(وَرَدَّ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا بِغَيْظِهِمْ لَمْ يَنالُوا خَيْراً): the wāw is a conjunction; (رد الله الذين كفروا) is conjoined to what precedes, and is a past verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; the clause (كفروا) is the ṣila of the relative noun — they are the Confederates. (بغيظهم) is a ḥāl (circumstantial), i.e. enraged; you may also make it a second object of (رد). The clause (لم ينالوا خيرا) is a second ḥāl, or a ḥāl from the first ḥāl, so that they are nested (mutadākhila). (وَكَفَى اللَّهُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ الْقِتالَ وَكانَ اللَّهُ قَوِيًّا عَزِيزاً): the wāw is a conjunction; (كفى الله المؤمنين) is a verb, its fāʿil and its first mafʿūl bihi, and (القتال) is the second mafʿūl bihi, because (كفى) here means "protected" (وقى), and in that case it is transitive to two objects; the discussion of (كفى) has passed in detail. (كان) with its noun and its two khabars.
(وَأَنْزَلَ الَّذِينَ ظاهَرُوهُمْ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتابِ مِنْ صَياصِيهِمْ): the wāw is a conjunction; (أنزل) is a past verb whose fāʿil is latent, referring to Allah; (الذين) is the mafʿūl bihi, and the clause (ظاهروهم) is the ṣila; (من أهل الكتاب) is a ḥāl; (من صياصيهم) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (أنزل). You may also make the speech resumptive, introduced [Translator's note: the source has «مسوفا», a misprint for «مسوقا»] to begin narrating the story of the campaign against the Banū Qurayẓa, a summary of which will come in the section on benefits. (وَقَذَفَ فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ الرُّعْبَ فَرِيقاً تَقْتُلُونَ وَتَأْسِرُونَ فَرِيقاً): (وقذف) is conjoined to (أنزل); (في قلوبهم) is attached to (قذف); (الرعب) is the mafʿūl bihi of (قذف); (فريقا) is a fronted object of (تقتلون); (تأسرون فريقا) is a verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi. (وَأَوْرَثَكُمْ أَرْضَهُمْ وَدِيارَهُمْ وَأَمْوالَهُمْ وَأَرْضاً لَمْ تَطَؤُها وَكانَ اللَّهُ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيراً):
(أورثكم) is a verb, a latent fāʿil and the first mafʿūl bihi; (أرضهم) is the second mafʿūl bihi; (ديارهم), (أموالهم) and (أرضا) are conjoined to (أرضهم); the clause (لم تطئوها) is an adjective of (أرضا); (كان) with its noun and its khabar. What is meant by it [the land not yet trodden] is the lands they conquered later.

* Rhetoric:
In His saying «ورد الذين كفروا بغيظهم ...» — the verse — there is the device of al-munāsaba (congruity). Allusion to this device has preceded, and that it is of two kinds: congruity in meanings and congruity in wording. What occurs in this verse is of the first kind, because had the speech been confined to what precedes the verse-ending, it would have led some weak people to imagine that this report agrees with the belief of the disbelievers that the wind which arose was the cause of their returning disappointed and of the believers being spared fighting them — that the wind merely arose by chance, as it arises in some of their battles and in their fighting one another — and they would have thought that it was not from Allah. So a safeguard (iḥtirās) was provided by the coming of the verse-ending, in which He, glory be to Him, reported that He is Strong, Mighty, able by His strength to do every impossible thing, that His party is the victorious one, and that by His power He makes victory come to the believers in various forms, to increase them in faith and steadfastness. He grants them victory once through fighting, as on the day of Badr; at another time through the wind, as on the day of the Confederates; at another through terror, as with the Banū al-Naḍīr; sometimes He gives victory against them first and makes the final outcome theirs at last, as on the day of Uḥud; and sometimes He shows them that numbers were not and never will be everything in battle, and how many a small band has overcome a large band, so that they may realise that victory is only from Allah, as on the day of Ḥunayn. This is among the most splendid things with which speech is adorned.

* Benefits:
A summary of the story of the campaign against the Banū Qurayẓa:
On the morning after the night in which the Confederates were routed, Allah revealed to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: "Allah commands you to march to the Banū Qurayẓa." So he proclaimed among the people: "Whoever hears and obeys, let him not pray the ʿaṣr prayer except among the Banū Qurayẓa." Many of the people did not pray ʿaṣr until after the late ʿishāʾ. He besieged them twenty-five nights until the siege exhausted them, and Allah cast terror into their hearts. The Prophet said to them: "Will you come down to my judgment?" They refused. He said: "Will you come down to the judgment of Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, the chief of al-Aws?" They accepted him. He judged concerning them and said: "I judge that the men be killed, the property divided, and the children and women taken captive." The Prophet said: "You have judged with the judgment of Allah." Then he brought them down, dug a trench in the market of Medina, brought them forward and struck their necks; they numbered from eight hundred to nine hundred.
[Volume Eight]
[Continuation of Sūrat al-Aḥzāb]

dervis-irab:69-73.t:
* Vocabulary:
(وَجِيهاً): al-wajīh is the chief of the people, possessed of standing (jāh) and eminence (wajāha). One says وجه الرجل يوجه وجاهة, so he is wajīh.
(سَدِيداً): right. One says سدّ يسدّ, of the pattern ḍaraba, [meaning] it became sound. Al-sadād, with fatḥa on the sīn, is aiming at the truth and speaking with justice. As for al-sidād, with kasra, it is anything with which you stop up something, like the stopper of a bottle (sidād al-qārūra) and the defence of a frontier (sidād al-thaghr). It is reported in the accounts of the grammarians that al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl al-Māzinī gained eighty thousand dirhams by teaching this one letter. He said: I used to visit al-Maʾmūn in his evening gatherings. One night I came in wearing a patched shirt, and he said: "O Naḍr, what is this austerity, that you come before the Commander of the Faithful in these rags?" I said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I am a weak old man and the heat of Marw is severe, so I cool myself with these rags."
He said: "No, rather you are an austere man." Then we fell into conversation, and he brought up the mention of women and said: "Hushaym related to us from Mujālid, from al-Shaʿbī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: When a man marries a woman for her religion and her beauty, there is in her sadād min ʿawaz (a remedy for need)" — and he pronounced it with fatḥa on the sīn. [Al-Naḍr] said: I said: "Hushaym spoke truly, O Commander of the Faithful. ʿAwf ibn Abī Jamīla related to us from al-Ḥasan, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: When a man marries a woman for her religion and her beauty, there is in her sidād min ʿawaz." He said: al-Maʾmūn was reclining, and he sat up straight and said: "O Naḍr, how did you say sidād?" I said: "Because sadād here is a solecism." He said: "Do you accuse me of a solecism?" I said: "It was only Hushaym who committed the solecism — he was much given to solecisms — and the Commander of the Faithful followed his wording." He said: "What is the difference between them?" I said: "Sadād, with fatḥa, is moderation in religion and in the way; with kasra it is sufficiency (bulgha), and everything with which you stop up something is a sidāda." He said: "Do the Arabs know that?" I said: "Yes; here is al-ʿArjī saying:
أضاعوني وأي فتى أضاعوا ... ليوم كريهة وسداد ثغر
(They lost me — and what a young man they lost, for a day of hardship and the defence of a frontier!)"
Al-Maʾmūn said: "May Allah disgrace whoever has no culture!" He bowed his head for a long while, then said:
"What is your property, O Naḍr?" I said: "A small plot of land of mine in Marw, from which I take sips [i.e. a little at a time]." He said: "Shall we not give you some wealth along with it?" I said: "I am indeed in need of that." He said: he took a sheet, and I did not know what he was writing. Then he said: "How do you say when you order [a letter] to be dusted?" [I said:] "أتربْ." He said: "Then it is what?" I said: "مترب." He said: "And from clay?" I said: "طِنْه." He said: "Then it is what?" I said: "مطين." He said: "This is better than the first." Then he said: "Boy, dust it and seal it with clay." Then he led us in the ʿIshāʾ prayer and said to his servant: "Go with him to al-Faḍl ibn Sahl." He said: When al-Faḍl read the letter he said: "O Naḍr, the Commander of the Faithful has ordered fifty thousand dirhams for you." Then al-Faḍl ordered thirty thousand for me, so I took eighty thousand dirhams for one letter that was learned from me. Someone has versified this difference between the fatḥa and the kasra, mentioning the ḍamma too, saying:
والاستقامة هي السّد ... وبلغة من عيش السّداد
وجمع سدّة أتى سداد ... وهي زكام مانع للنشر
(Rectitude is al-sadād, and sufficiency of livelihood is al-sidād; and the plural of sudda comes as sudād, which is a cold that blocks smelling.)
In al-Qāmūs he said: al-sudād: a disease in the nose that prevents smelling the air (تنشم الريح).
(أَشْفَقْنَ): they feared.

* I'rab:
(يا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تَكُونُوا كَالَّذِينَ آذَوْا مُوسى): لا is prohibitive; تكونوا is a defective imperfect verb, jussive (majzūm) by لا; the wāw is its noun, and كالذين its khabar (predicate), on the basis that the kāf is a noun meaning "like" and الذين is the muḍāf ilayhi. The kāf may also be a preposition, the preposition and its genitive noun being the khabar of تكونوا. The clause آذوا موسى is the ṣila (relative clause). It has been said that they accused him of a defect in his body, leprosy or a scrotal hernia; the ḥadīth of Muslim on this subject will come in the Benefits section.
(فَبَرَّأَهُ اللَّهُ مِمَّا قالُوا وَكانَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ وَجِيهاً): the fāʾ is a conjunction; برأه الله is a verb, a fronted mafʿūl bihi (direct object) and a postponed fāʿil (agent). مما: ما may be relative or maṣdarī, i.e. from what they said or from their saying; in either case it is attached (mutaʿalliq) to براءة [Translator's note: so in the source; the verb in the verse is برّأه]. The wāw is a conjunction; كان is a defective past verb, and its noun is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "هو", referring to Moses. عند الله is attached to وجيها, and وجيها is the khabar of كان.
(يا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَقُولُوا قَوْلًا سَدِيداً): a resumptive clause, introduced to confirm what preceded. اتقوا الله is an imperative verb, its fāʿil and its object; قولوا is an imperative verb and its fāʿil; قولا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) and سديدا a naʿt (adjective).
(يُصْلِحْ لَكُمْ أَعْمالَكُمْ وَيَغْفِرْ لَكُمْ ذُنُوبَكُمْ): يصلح is jussive as the answer to the request. لكم is attached to يصلح; أعمالكم is a mafʿūl bihi; the clause ويغفر لكم ذنوبكم is conjoined to the preceding clause.
(وَمَنْ يُطِعِ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ فَقَدْ فازَ فَوْزاً عَظِيماً): the wāw is resumptive; من is a jussive conditional noun and a mubtadaʾ (subject); يطع الله is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ). فقد: the fāʾ links the apodosis because it is joined with قد. فاز is a past verb whose fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "هو", referring to من; فوزا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq and عظيما a naʿt; the clause is in the position of the jussive as the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ).
(إِنَّا عَرَضْنَا الْأَمانَةَ عَلَى السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَالْجِبالِ): a resumptive statement, introduced to draw attention to the importance of the trust and to magnify its matter; a fuller treatment of it will come in the Rhetoric section. إن and its noun, and the clause عرضنا is its khabar; الأمانة is the object of عرضنا; على السموات is attached to عرضنا, and what follows is conjoined to السموات.
(فَأَبَيْنَ أَنْ يَحْمِلْنَها وَأَشْفَقْنَ مِنْها): the fāʾ is a conjunction; أبين is a past verb and its fāʿil; أن and what falls within its scope is the object of أبين; أشفقن is conjoined to أبين, and منها is attached to أشفقن.
(وَحَمَلَهَا الْإِنْسانُ إِنَّهُ كانَ ظَلُوماً جَهُولًا): the wāw is a conjunction; حملها is a past verb and a fronted mafʿūl bihi, and الإنسان a postponed fāʿil. إن and its noun, and the clause كان is its khabar; ظلوما is its [i.e. كان's] first khabar and جهولا its second khabar.
(لِيُعَذِّبَ اللَّهُ الْمُنافِقِينَ وَالْمُنافِقاتِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ وَالْمُشْرِكاتِ): the lām is attached to حملها, or, it is said, to عرضنا. The lām is causal, by way of figurative usage, because the punishment is the result of bearing the trust. يعذب is an imperfect verb, accusative by an implied أن after the lām; الله is the fāʿil, المنافقين is a mafʿūl bihi, and what follows is conjoined to it.
(وَيَتُوبَ اللَّهُ عَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمُؤْمِناتِ وَكانَ اللَّهُ غَفُوراً رَحِيماً): ويتوب الله is conjoined to يعذب الله; على المؤمنين is attached to يتوب; المؤمنات is conjoined to المؤمنين; كان, its noun and its two khabars.

* Rhetoric:
Tamthīl (representational analogy):
In His words «إنا عرضنا الأمانة على السموات etc.» there is the device of tamthīl. What is meant by the trust is obedience in general, and there is no room for restricting it. Its being offered to the heavens, the earth and the mountains is a representation, so it is an istiʿāra tamthīliyya (representational metaphor), which has been discussed before. ʿAbd al-Qāhir, however, made a distinction between istiʿāra and tamthīl. The first distinction he draws between them is that istiʿāra occurs in a single word that is transferred from its original linguistic meaning and applied to what it was not coined for, because of a resemblance between what it is transferred to and what it is transferred from: if you say "I saw a lion", meaning the brave man, the istiʿāra is in the word "lion". Tamthīl, on the other hand, is a comparison drawn from a combination of things that can only be expressed in a sentence or more, and you may find the words in the sentences from which it is formed running according to their original, literal meanings in the language. Moreover, the tamthīl here rests on something imagined in the mind; for offering the trust to inanimate things, and their refusal and fear, is impossible in itself and not sound. So the thing compared to is not rationally conceivable; rather, you imagine the state of religious obligation, in its difficulty and the heaviness of its burden, by its hypothetical state: were it offered to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, they would refuse to bear it and fear it. The trust, which is acts of obedience, is as if it were riding upon the believer and he were bearing it. Do you not see that they say: "debts have ridden him", and "I have a right upon him"? When he fulfils them, they no longer ride him, nor is he bearing them. Similar is their saying: "No client possesses help for a client", meaning that he gives his help freely and is generous with it, and does not hold it back as the forsaker holds it back, in the manner of the saying of al-Quṭāmī — or, it is said, Dhū al-Rumma:
أخوك الذي لا تملك الحس نفسه ... وترفض عند المحفظات الكتائف
(Your brother is he whose soul does not hold back tenderness, and whose rancours scatter when angering things occur.)
That is, he does not hold back tenderness and sympathy as the miserly owner holds what is in his hand; rather he gives it and is generous with it. حسّ له حسا: he felt tenderness and sympathy for him. Al-ḥiss is also intelligence, management and considering the consequences. Al-irfiḍāḍ is from sprinkling and scattering.
أحفظه إحفاظا [he angered him], so al-muḥfiẓāt are the angering things; al-katāʾif is the plural of katīfa, which is rancour, resentment and spite. He says: he is your brother whose soul does not hold back mercy but gives it to you; or: whose soul cannot manage with deliberation, so that he rushes to you suddenly, and he trembles and his rancours on your side vanish when things that anger you occur, because they anger him too.

* Benefits:
These verses were revealed concerning Zayd and Zaynab, the talk that circulated among people about it, and the rumours spread by some rumour-mongers. Various views have been given concerning the harm done to Moses. Muslim narrated from Abū Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
"The Children of Israel used to bathe naked, looking at one another's private parts, while Moses, upon him be peace, used to bathe alone. They said: By Allah, nothing prevents Moses from bathing with us except that he has a scrotal hernia (ādar). He said: So one day he went to bathe and put his garment on a stone, and the stone fled with his garment. He said: Moses, upon him be peace, began running after it, saying: My garment, O stone! My garment, O stone! until the Children of Israel looked at Moses' private parts and said: By Allah, there is nothing wrong with Moses. Then the stone stopped, until they had looked at him. He said: He took his garment and covered himself with it, and set about striking the stone." Abū Hurayra said: "By Allah, there are six or seven scars on it from Moses' striking." In al-Qāmūs: «al-nadba is the trace of a wound remaining on the skin; the plural is nadab, like shajara and shajar, and andāb and nudūb». Al-udra, with ḍamma on the hamza, sukūn on the undotted dāl and fatḥa on the rāʾ, is a disease by which the testicles swell and become very large because of matter or thick wind pouring into them; a man who is ādar, with the long alif like ādam, has udra.

dervis-irab:28-33.t:
* Vocabulary:
(ضِعْفَيْنِ): dual of (ضعف), with kasra on the ḍād. One says: the ḍiʿf of a thing is its like in quantity, or its like plus an unlimited increase; so their saying "you have its ḍiʿf" means you have twice it, or three times it, or more. In al-Miṣbāḥ: «The ḍiʿf of a thing is its like; its two ḍiʿfs are twice it; its aḍʿāf are multiples of it. Al-Khalīl said: taḍʿīf is that the base of a thing is increased so that it is made twice it or more; likewise al-aḍʿāf and al-muḍāʿafa. Al-Azharī said: al-ḍiʿf in the speech of the Arabs is the like — this is the original sense — then ḍiʿf came to be used for the like and more, with no limit to the increase. One says "this is the ḍiʿf of this", i.e. its like, and "these are its two ḍiʿfs", i.e. twice it. He said: and it is allowed in the speech of the Arabs to say "this is its ḍiʿf", meaning twice it or three times it, because ḍiʿf is an unlimited increase. So if someone says in a bequest "give him the ḍiʿf of my son's share", he is given twice it; and if he says "its two ḍiʿfs", he is given three times it. So if the son gets a hundred, he is given two hundred for "ḍiʿf" and three hundred for "two ḍiʿfs". People's custom and usage run on this, and the bequest is interpreted according to custom, not according to the subtleties of language.» Further, ḍaʿf with fatḥa on the ḍād, ḍiʿf with kasra and ḍuʿf with ḍamma have meanings that someone put into verse thus:
في الرأي والعقل يكون الضّعف ... والوهن في الجسم فذاك الضّعف
زيادة المثل كذا والضّعف ... جمع ضعيف وهو شاكي الضر
(Weakness in opinion and mind is ḍaʿf; feebleness in the body is ḍuʿf; the increase of the like is ḍiʿf; and ḍiʿāf [Translator's note: the vocalisation is not marked in the source] is the plural of ḍaʿīf, one who complains of harm.)
(كَأَحَدٍ مِنَ النِّساءِ): (أحد) — as al-Zamakhsharī says — is originally in the sense of وحد, i.e. "one" (الواحد); then it was set in general negation, in which masculine and feminine, the one and what is beyond it, are all equal. Others replied to him, saying: as for his saying that أحد is originally in the sense of وحد, i.e. one, that is correct; but as for his saying "and what is beyond it", that is not correct, because what is used in general negation has a meaning other than that of واحد; for واحد is applied to everything characterised by oneness, whereas the أحد used in general negation is specific to rational beings. They are also distinguished in that the one specific to negation is a primitive noun (jāmid) while this one is an adjective; and also the one specific to negation is specific to rational beings while this one is not. As for the sense of negation, it is evident, according to what al-Zamakhsharī said, as applying to the whole.
In al-Itqān: Abū Ḥātim said: أحد is a more complete noun than واحد. Do you not see that if you say "no واحد can stand up to so-and-so", it is possible in meaning that two could stand up to him, unlike your saying "no أحد can stand up to him"? And أحد has a particularity not found in واحد: you say "there is no أحد in the house", and it covers all creatures — beasts, birds, wild animals and humans — thus including people and others; unlike your saying "there is no واحد in the house", which is specific to human beings to the exclusion of others. He said: أحد also comes in the speech of the Arabs in the sense of واحد, and is then used in affirmation and negation, as in «قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ», i.e. one; «أَيَحْسَبُ أَنْ لَنْ يَقْدِرَ عَلَيْهِ أَحَدٌ»; «فَما مِنْكُمْ مِنْ أَحَدٍ»; and "no one (أحد) has merit over anyone (أحد)". أحد is used for masculine and feminine; the Exalted said: «لَسْتُنَّ كَأَحَدٍ مِنَ النِّساءِ», unlike واحد, for one does not say كواحد من النساء but كواحدة. I say: and for this reason it was described [with a plural] in His saying, the Exalted, «فما منكم من أحد عنه حاجزين», unlike واحد. أحد has a plural from its own root, namely الأحدون and الآحاد, whereas واحد has no plural from its own root — one does not say واحدون, but rather اثنان, ثلاثة. And أحد cannot enter into multiplication, counting, division or any arithmetic, unlike واحد.
(وَقَرْنَ فِي بُيُوتِكُنَّ): from القرار, i.e. staying firm. Its origin is اقررن, with kasra or fatḥa on the rāʾ, from قررت with fatḥa or kasra on the rāʾ; the vowel of the rāʾ was transferred to the qāf, and the rāʾ was dropped together with the connecting hamza. In al-Qāmūs: «قرّ بالمكان يقرّ, with kasra and fatḥa, qarāran, qurūran, qarran and taqirratan: he stayed firm and settled, like استقرّ.»
(تَبَرَّجْنَ): with one of the two tāʾs dropped; its origin is تتبرجن, i.e. strut in your walk. In al-Qāmūs: «تبرجت المرأة: the woman displayed her adornment and her charms to strangers.»
(الْجاهِلِيَّةِ): the state of ignorance and idolatry in the land of the Arabs before Islam, or the period preceding it. More discussion of "the first jāhiliyya" will come in the section on benefits.

* I'rab:
(يا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ قُلْ لِأَزْواجِكَ إِنْ كُنْتُنَّ تُرِدْنَ الْحَياةَ الدُّنْيا وَزِينَتَها): resumptive speech, introduced to establish the position of Islam regarding the wives of the Prophet and woman in general. (قل) is an imperative verb whose fāʿil (agent) is latent, its implied form being "you"; (لأزواجك) is attached to (mutaʿalliq) (قل). The names of the Prophet's wives will come in the section on benefits. (إن) is conditional; (كنتن) is a defective past verb in the position of a jussive as the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ); the tāʾ is its noun and the nūn is the sign of the feminine. The choice was offered to sound the depths of their souls, so that if they chose this world he would part from them. The clause (تردن) is the khabar (predicate) of (كان), the nūn being its fāʿil; (الحياة الدنيا) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object), and (زينتها) is conjoined to (الحياة). (فَتَعالَيْنَ أُمَتِّعْكُنَّ وَأُسَرِّحْكُنَّ سَراحاً جَمِيلًا): the fāʾ links the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ), because it came as a clause of request; (تعالين) is an imperative verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on sukūn, and the nūn is the fāʿil; (أمتعكن) is jussive (majzūm) because it is the answer to the request; (أسرحكن) is conjoined to (أمتعكن); (سراحا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) and (جميلا) an adjective. This is preferable to the view that (أمتعكن) is jussive as the apodosis of the condition, with what lies between the condition and its requital being parenthetical. (وَإِنْ كُنْتُنَّ تُرِدْنَ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ وَالدَّارَ الْآخِرَةَ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ أَعَدَّ لِلْمُحْسِناتِ مِنْكُنَّ أَجْراً عَظِيماً): the wāw is a conjunction; (إن) is conditional; (كنتن) is a defective past verb in the position of a jussive as the protasis; the tāʾ is its noun and the clause (تردن) its khabar, the nūn being the fāʿil of (تردن); (الله) is the mafʿūl bihi, (رسوله) is conjoined to it, and (الدار الآخرة) is also conjoined. The fāʾ is linking; (إن) with its noun, and the clause (أعد للمحسنات) is its khabar; (منكن) is a ḥāl (circumstantial); (أجرا) is the mafʿūl bihi and (عظيما) an adjective.
(يا نِساءَ النَّبِيِّ مَنْ يَأْتِ مِنْكُنَّ بِفاحِشَةٍ مُبَيِّنَةٍ يُضاعَفْ لَهَا الْعَذابُ ضِعْفَيْنِ): (يا) is a vocative particle and (نساء النبي) a muḍāf vocative. (من) is a jussive conditional noun in the position of a nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject); (يأت) is the protasis, the sign of its jussive being the dropping of the weak letter; (منكن) is a ḥāl; (بفاحشة) is attached to (يأت). (يضاعف) is the apodosis, jussive, the sign of its jussive being the sukūn; (لها) is attached to (يضاعف); (العذاب) is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) of (يضاعف), and (ضعفين) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq. (وَكانَ ذلِكَ عَلَى اللَّهِ يَسِيراً): the wāw is circumstantial or resumptive; (كان) with its noun; (على الله) is attached to (يسيرا), and (يسيرا) is the khabar of (كان). (وَمَنْ يَقْنُتْ مِنْكُنَّ لِلَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ وَتَعْمَلْ صالِحاً نُؤْتِها أَجْرَها مَرَّتَيْنِ): conjoined to what precedes and parallel to what came before it in its i'rab; (أجرها) is the second mafʿūl bihi of (نؤتها), and (مرتين) is accusative as a mafʿūl muṭlaq or as an adverb of time. (وَأَعْتَدْنا لَها رِزْقاً كَرِيماً): the wāw is a conjunction; (أعتدنا) is a past verb and its fāʿil; (لها) is attached to (أعتدنا); (رزقا) is the mafʿūl bihi and (كريما) an adjective.
(يا نِساءَ النَّبِيِّ لَسْتُنَّ كَأَحَدٍ مِنَ النِّساءِ إِنِ اتَّقَيْتُنَّ): (لستن): (ليس), the tāʾ is its noun and the nūn is the sign of the feminine plural; (كأحد) is the khabar of (لستن), and (من النساء) is an adjective of (أحد). (إن) is conditional; (اتقيتن) is a past verb and its fāʿil, in the position of a jussive as the protasis, and the apodosis is omitted, indicated by what precedes, i.e. "then you are greater". On this view His saying (فَلا تَخْضَعْنَ بِالْقَوْلِ) is resumptive, explaining the cause of the denial of equality. It is also possible that the fāʾ is linking, and that the clause (لا تخضعن) is in the position of a jussive as the apodosis; (بالقول) is a ḥāl, or attached to (تخضعن).
(فَيَطْمَعَ الَّذِي فِي قَلْبِهِ مَرَضٌ وَقُلْنَ قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفاً): the fāʾ is causal; (يطمع) is an imperfect verb, accusative (manṣūb) by an implied (أن) after the causal fāʾ preceded by a prohibition; (الذي) is the fāʿil of (يطمع); (في قلبه) is attached to an omitted fronted khabar and (مرض) is a delayed mubtadaʾ, the clause being the ṣila (relative clause). (وقلن): the wāw is a conjunction, (قلن) is an imperative verb, and the nūn is the fāʿil; (قولا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq clarifying the kind, and (معروفا) an adjective. (وَقَرْنَ فِي بُيُوتِكُنَّ وَلا تَبَرَّجْنَ تَبَرُّجَ الْجاهِلِيَّةِ الْأُولى): conjoined to what precedes; (قرن) is an imperative verb — it has been covered in the section on vocabulary — and (في بيوتكن) is attached to it. (لا تبرجن) is a prohibition; (تبرج الجاهلية) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq, and (الأولى) is the naʿt (adjective) of (الجاهلية). (وَأَقِمْنَ الصَّلاةَ وَآتِينَ الزَّكاةَ وَأَطِعْنَ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ): conjoined to (قرن في بيوتكن).
(إِنَّما يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ لِيُذْهِبَ عَنْكُمُ الرِّجْسَ أَهْلَ الْبَيْتِ وَيُطَهِّرَكُمْ تَطْهِيراً): (إنما) is the restraining particle (mā al-kāffa) with the restrained (inna); (يريد الله) is an imperfect verb and its fāʿil. (ليذهب): the lām is of cause, and (يذهب) is an imperfect verb, accusative by an implied (أن) after the lām. The clause (إنما يريد) is a causal explanation of all that precedes. The preposition with its genitive noun, i.e. (ليذهب), is attached to (يريد); (عنكم) is attached to (يذهب); (الرجس) is the mafʿūl bihi. (أهل البيت) is accusative by specification for praise (ikhtiṣāṣ), i.e. "I mean specifically the people of the House"; you may also make it a vocative with the particle omitted, or a badal (substitute) from the kāf — al-Mubarrad objected to this, that a badal from the person addressed is not permissible. (يطهركم) is conjoined to (يذهب), and (تطهيرا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq.

* Benefits:
1- The scaremongering of the malicious about the Prophet's plural marriages:
We will speak at length on this matter, because it has raised doubts among the malicious and the partisan among the Orientalists and the defamers of Islam. In the course of their fabrications and scaremongering they have said that the Prophet's plurality of wives is incompatible with the qualities of prophethood and contrary to what should characterise the bearers of a call and the guides of souls. One of the Orientalists said, word for word: "Nine wives are proof of excessive sexual inclination." They forgot, or feigned to forget, that there is no shame for a great man in loving woman and feeling her favour; and there is no instinct deeper in the natures of living beings in general than the instinct of the two sexes and the meeting of male and female. Yes, there may be shame if this love overflows until it takes the great man off the straight path and distracts him from what he is concerned with of guidance. And nothing shows him ﷺ farther from surrendering to the whims of sensual pleasure than that he was on the point of divorcing his wives, or offering them the choice of divorce, because they asked him for more maintenance. History relates that Abū Bakr went to him one day seeking permission to enter, and found people sitting, none of them being given permission. Then Abū Bakr entered, and ʿUmar after him, and he found the Prophet sitting with his wives around him, gloomy and silent. Abū Bakr wanted to say something to cheer him up, so he said:
"O Messenger of Allah, if only you had seen the daughter of Khārija! She asked me for maintenance, so I got up and struck her on the neck." The Prophet laughed and said: "They are around me, as you see, asking me for maintenance." So Abū Bakr got up to ʿĀʾisha to strike her on the neck, and ʿUmar got up to Ḥafṣa to strike her on the neck, both saying: "Do you ask the Messenger of Allah [Translator's note: the source has «رسال الله», a misprint] for what he does not have?" They said: "By Allah, we will not ask the Messenger of Allah for anything he does not have." Then the Messenger withdrew from them for a month, or twenty-nine days, after which the verse containing the choice came down, namely «يا أيها النبي قل لأزواجك» — the verse. The Messenger began with ʿĀʾisha and said to her:
"ʿĀʾisha, I want to put a matter before you, and I would like you not to hasten in it until you consult your parents." She said: "And what is it, O Messenger of Allah?" He recited the verse to her. She said: "Is it concerning you, O Messenger of Allah, that I should consult my parents? No — I choose Allah, His Messenger and the abode of the Hereafter." Then he offered the choice to all his wives, and they answered as ʿĀʾisha had answered, and contented themselves with the living they had — while many of the wives of the Muslims enjoyed a more comfortable one. What does this indicate? Had the Prophet wished, he would have showered them with comfort and drowned them in splendid adornment, wondrous jewellery and the finest pleasures. Is this turning away from that the act of someone surrendered to sensual pleasures, consumed by love of women? And when he married the first of his wives — Khadīja — it was not the pleasures of beauty that dominated this marriage or prompted it, for he married her when she was about forty and he about twenty-five; and he passed fifty and was granted the manifest victory with no wife but her, and no desire whatever to marry another appeared from him.
ʿĀʾisha once said to him: "Was Khadīja anything but an old woman, whom Allah has replaced for you with someone better than her?" He said to her angrily: "No, by Allah, Allah has not given me anyone better than her in exchange. She believed in me when people disbelieved, she affirmed my truth when people called me a liar, she consoled me with her wealth when people deprived me, and Allah granted me children from her and from no other woman."
Had it been the pleasures of beauty that dominated the Prophet's marriages after [Translator's note: the source repeats «بعد»] the death of Khadīja, the more fitting way to satisfy these pleasures would have been to gather to himself nine virgin girls renowned for the allure of beauty in Mecca, Medina and the Arabian Peninsula, who would have hastened to him, content and proud, with their guardians even more content and proud of this marriage-tie above which no marriage-tie could rise. But Muhammad never married a virgin other than ʿĀʾisha, and his marriage to her was not intended at the outset, until Khawla bint Ḥakīm made him desire it, she who proposed marriage to him after Khadīja's death.
ʿĀʾisha said: When Khadīja died, Khawla bint Ḥakīm, the wife of ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn, said to the Prophet: "O Messenger of Allah, will you not marry?" He said: "Whom?" She said: "If you wish, a virgin, and if you wish, a previously married woman." He said: "And who is the virgin?" She said: "The daughter of the dearest of people to you, ʿĀʾisha bint Abī Bakr." He said: "And who is the previously married one?" She said:
"Sawda bint Zamʿa; she has believed in you and followed you."
Sawda then was the first of the women he married after the death of Khadīja. Her first husband — her paternal cousin — had died after returning from the emigration to Abyssinia. She was among the earliest women to embrace Islam: she believed and left her family, and her husband escaped with her to Abyssinia, fleeing the polytheists' harassment of him and of her. When he died, nothing remained for her but to return to her family and be [treated as] an apostate (taṣbaʾ) and be persecuted, or to marry someone unsuited to her. So the Prophet took her to himself to protect her and to win over his enemies among her kin. Another marriage than this would have been more fitting for him had he looked to the pleasures of beauty and inclined to enjoyment.
The Prophet had another wife distinguished by radiance, youth and freshness: Zaynab bint Jaḥsh, his paternal aunt's daughter, whom he had married to Zayd ibn Ḥāritha at his command and without her consent, because she disdained — given what she was in lineage and kinship to the Messenger of Allah — being married to a freed slave. In her case, too, the pleasures of beauty had no sway in the Prophet's marrying her after Zayd divorced her and reconciliation between them proved impossible. Her story will come in full, supported by a complete analysis of it.
As for the rest of his wives, there is not one of them but that his marriage to her had a reason of public interest.

A summary of the names of his wives:
Ibn al-Kalbī said: The Prophet ﷺ married fifteen women, consummated marriage with thirteen, had eleven at one time, and died leaving nine. The first of them was Khadīja bint Khuwaylid. Before him she had been married to ʿAtīq ibn ʿĀbid ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn Makhzūm, who died leaving her; after him Abū Hāla ibn Zurāra ibn al-Nabbāsh al-Tamīmī married her, and she bore him Hind; then he died leaving her, and after him the Prophet married her, and she bore him eight:
al-Qāsim, al-Ṭayyib, al-Ṭāhir, ʿAbd Allāh, Zaynab, Ruqayya, Umm Kulthūm and Fāṭima.
The males died young; the females reached maturity, married and bore children. He married no one else while Khadīja was alive, and her death was three years before the Hijra. After her came Sawda bint Zamʿa — and it is said ʿĀʾisha, who was six years old; he consummated the marriage with her in Medina when she was nine, and died leaving her when she was eighteen; she died in the year fifty-eight. As for Sawda, she was a previously married woman; before him she had been married to al-Sakrān ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Shams, who died leaving her, and the Messenger of Allah succeeded him as her husband and consummated the marriage with her in Mecca. After her he married Ḥafṣa bint ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb; before him she had been married to Khunays ibn Ḥudhāfa al-Sahmī, who had fought at Badr; she died in Medina during the caliphate of ʿUthmān. After her he married Umm Salama, daughter of Abū Umayya, al-Makhzūmiyya; before him she had been married to Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Asad al-Makhzūmī, who fought at Badr and was wounded on the day of Uḥud and died leaving her; the Messenger of Allah married her before the Confederates. Then he married Zaynab bint Khuzayma of the Banū ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa, who was called "the mother of the poor"; she died during his lifetime, and no one besides her and Khadīja died during his lifetime; before him Zaynab had been married to al-Ṭufayl ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. Then he married Juwayriya [Translator's note: the source writes «جورية»], daughter of al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Ḍirār al-Khuzāʿiyya of the Banū al-Muṣṭaliq, who had been married to Mālik ibn Ṣafwān. Then he married Umm Ḥabība bint Abī Sufyān ibn Ḥarb; before him she had been married to ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Jaḥsh [Translator's note: the source has «عبد الله بن جحش»; the husband who became a Christian in Abyssinia is usually named ʿUbayd Allāh], who was among the emigrants to Abyssinia, became a Christian and died there. The Messenger of Allah sent to the Negus, who asked for her hand on his behalf, and he married her while she was in Abyssinia, the Negus paying the dower to her on behalf of the Messenger of Allah; she died during the caliphate of her brother Muʿāwiya. Then he married Zaynab bint Jaḥsh (her story will come). Then in the year of Khaybar he married Ṣafiyya bint Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab. Then he married Maymūna, daughter of al-Ḥārith, al-Hilāliyya; before him she had been married to ʿUmayr ibn ʿAmr al-Thaqafī, who died leaving her, then Abū Zuhayr ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā succeeded him, then the Messenger of Allah; she was the maternal aunt of Ibn ʿAbbās and of Khālid ibn al-Walīd. Then he married a woman of the Banū Kulayb called Shāh [Translator's note: the source writes «شاة»] bint Rifāʿa — and it is said Sanā bint al-Ṣalt, and it is said the daughter of al-Ṣalt ibn Ḥabīb — who died before he consummated the marriage. And it is said al-Shanbāʾ, with whom he consummated the marriage; when his son Ibrāhīm died, she said: "Had he been a prophet, his child would not have died", so he divorced her. Then he married Ghaziyya bint Jābir al-Kilābiyya. Ibn al-Kalbī said: Ghaziyya is Umm Sharīk; when she came to the Prophet and he wanted to be alone with her, she sought refuge from him, so he sent her back. Then he married al-ʿĀliya, daughter of Ẓabyān, joined her [to his household], then parted from her. Then he married Qutayla, daughter of Qays, the sister of al-Ashʿath; he died before consummating the marriage with her, and she apostatised. Then he married Fāṭima, daughter of al-Ḍaḥḥāk. And it is said he married Khawla, daughter of al-Hudhayl ibn Hubayra; and Laylā, daughter of al-Ḥaṭīm, offered herself to him, and he married her and parted from her.
Ibn al-Kalbī said: As for the women the Prophet sought in marriage but did not marry: Umm Hāniʾ bint Abī Ṭālib, whom he sought but did not marry; Ḍubāʿa, daughter of ʿĀmir, of the Banū Qushayr; Ṣafiyya bint Bashāma, al-Aʿwar al-ʿAnbarī [Translator's note: so in the source]; Umm Ḥabība, daughter of his uncle al-ʿAbbās — he found that al-ʿAbbās was his foster-brother, so he left her; and Jamra, daughter of al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Ḥāritha, whom he sought in marriage, and her father said: "There is something wrong with her" — though she had no ailment — and he went back to her and found that she had become leprous.
As for his concubines: Māriya, daughter of Shamʿūn, the Copt [Translator's note: the source has «القطبية», for «القبطية»], who bore him Ibrāhīm; Rayḥāna, daughter of Zayd, of Qurayẓa — it is said she was of the Banū al-Naḍīr; another whom Zaynab bint Jaḥsh gave to him, whose name was Nafīsa; and a fourth whom he obtained in some captivity, whose name is not known.
In al-Mawāhib there is another report in which the names differ somewhat; it would take us too long to quote it, so let whoever wishes refer to it.
Restoring the honour of those humbled after being honoured was the Prophet's practice in dealing with all people, especially women, whose hearts are broken by humiliation after losing their protectors and nearest kin. For this reason he gave Ṣafiyya the Israelite, the lady of the Banū Qurayẓa, the choice between sending her to her family and freeing her and marrying her, and she chose to marry him.
Moreover, a review of the married life of Muhammad, upon him be blessing and peace, reveals to us the reasons that prompted him to marry them and to gather this number of them. There is no blame on a man of sound nature in seeking enjoyment in his marriage; but the fact is that enjoyment was never foremost in the Prophet's consideration when he considered choosing any one of his wives, before the call, after it, or after passing middle age. Rather, the choice was entirely according to their need for honourable shelter, or according to the greater interest that required a tie of kinship between him and the chiefs of the Arabs and the pillars of the Peninsula, of his friends and his enemies — with no exception in this trait for a single wife among all his wives, even the one he married as a young virgin marked by beauty, namely the Lady ʿĀʾisha.
2- The first jāhiliyya:
People have differed about "the first jāhiliyya". The most correct view is that there are two jāhiliyyas, a first and a last. The first is the ancient one, also called "the ignorant jāhiliyya" (al-jāhiliyya al-jahlāʾ), and it extends to the most distant times; the last jāhiliyya extends from the middle of the fifth century CE. In the first jāhiliyya a woman would wear a gown of pearls and walk in the middle of the road, displaying herself to men; so they were forbidden that.

dervis-irab:34-37.t:
* I'rab:
(وَاذْكُرْنَ ما يُتْلى فِي بُيُوتِكُنَّ مِنْ آياتِ اللَّهِ وَالْحِكْمَةِ): the wāw is a conjunction; (اذكرن) is an imperative verb and the nūn is its fāʿil (agent); (ما) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object), and the clause (يتلى) is the ṣila (relative clause). (يتلى) is an imperfect verb in the passive, and the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) is latent, referring to (ما); (في بيوتكن) is attached to (mutaʿalliq) (يتلى); (من آيات الله) is a ḥāl (circumstantial), and (الحكمة) is conjoined to (آيات الله).
(إِنَّ اللَّهَ كانَ لَطِيفاً خَبِيراً): (إن) with its noun, and the clause (كان) is its khabar (predicate); the noun of (كان) is latent, referring to Allah; (لطيفا) is its first khabar and (خبيرا) its second khabar.
(إِنَّ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَالْمُسْلِماتِ وَالْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمُؤْمِناتِ وَالْقانِتِينَ وَالْقانِتاتِ وَالصَّادِقِينَ وَالصَّادِقاتِ وَالصَّابِرِينَ وَالصَّابِراتِ وَالْخاشِعِينَ وَالْخاشِعاتِ وَالْمُتَصَدِّقِينَ وَالْمُتَصَدِّقاتِ وَالصَّائِمِينَ وَالصَّائِماتِ وَالْحافِظِينَ فُرُوجَهُمْ وَالْحافِظاتِ وَالذَّاكِرِينَ اللَّهَ كَثِيراً وَالذَّاكِراتِ أَعَدَّ اللَّهُ لَهُمْ مَغْفِرَةً وَأَجْراً عَظِيماً): resumptive speech, introduced to address women with what men are addressed with in the lofty matters of guidance and instruction. For the wives of the Prophet said: "Allah has mentioned men in His Book but has not mentioned women with good", and so it was revealed. (إن) with its noun, and what follows is conjoined to the noun up to His saying (والذاكرات). There is nothing in it calling for comment except His saying (فروجهم), which is the mafʿūl bihi of (الحافظين), and likewise His saying (والذاكرين الله), where the Divine Name is the mafʿūl bihi of (الذاكرين). The clause (أعد) is the khabar of (إن); (الله) is the fāʿil of (أعد); (لهم) is attached to (أعد); (أجرا) is the object of (أعد) and (عظيما) an adjective.
(وَما كانَ لِمُؤْمِنٍ وَلا مُؤْمِنَةٍ إِذا قَضَى اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ أَمْراً أَنْ يَكُونَ لَهُمُ الْخِيَرَةُ مِنْ أَمْرِهِمْ): the wāw is resumptive, and the speech is introduced to begin the story of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaḥsh, his sister Zaynab and Zayd ibn Ḥāritha; a lengthy discussion of it will come in the section on benefits. (ما) is negating; (كان) is a defective past verb; (لمؤمن) is the fronted khabar of (كان), and (ولا مؤمنة) is conjoined to (لمؤمن). (إذا) is a future adverb including the sense of condition; (قضى الله ورسوله) is its ṣila [Translator's note: so in the source, i.e. the clause to which إذا is annexed], and the apodosis (jawāb) is omitted, indicated by the preceding negation. You may also make (إذا) purely adverbial, so that it is attached to the notion of "being settled" to which the khabar of (كان) is attached. (أن يكون) is an interpreted maṣdar (verbal noun) that is the noun of (كان); (لهم) is the fronted khabar of (يكون) and (الخيرة) its delayed noun. (يكون) is masculine because the feminine is figurative, and it has been read with tāʾ (تكون). (من أمرهم) is a ḥāl from (الخيرة). (الخيرة) is the maṣdar of تخيّر, like الطيرة from تطيّر. The pronoun in (أمرهم) and in (لهم) is plural because they occur in the context of negation; it has preceded that an indefinite noun in the context of negation indicates generality, so as to include every believing man and believing woman — just as the masculine has been given precedence over the feminine. (وَمَنْ يَعْصِ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ فَقَدْ ضَلَّ ضَلالًا مُبِيناً): the wāw is a conjunction; (من) is conditional, the mubtadaʾ (subject); (يعص) is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ), jussive (majzūm) by the dropping of the weak letter, and the fāʿil of (يعص) is latent, its implied form being "he", referring to (من). The Divine Name is the mafʿūl bihi and (رسوله) is conjoined to it. The fāʾ links the apodosis because it is joined with (قد); (ضل) is a past verb whose fāʿil is also latent; (ضلالا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) and (مبينا) an adjective.
(وَإِذْ تَقُولُ لِلَّذِي أَنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَأَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِ أَمْسِكْ عَلَيْكَ زَوْجَكَ وَاتَّقِ اللَّهَ): conjoined to what preceded.
